Illustrative title: Retirement Security in a Changing Economy

Model précis: Retirement security depends not simply on accumulated savings but also on stable earnings, accessible institutions and systems that manage uncertainty. Traditional pensions assumed predictable employment, whereas irregular incomes and interrupted careers now make regular contributions difficult. Genuine financial inclusion therefore requires affordable, convenient and transparent arrangements that build trust. Policymakers must balance investment flexibility against market risk, guarantees against financial sustainability, and emergency withdrawals against future adequacy. Women, informal workers and those with interrupted careers face particular disadvantages, calling for inclusive yet administratively sustainable designs. Pension systems should consequently be assessed not only by enrolment or assets, but by their ability to provide dependable old-age income while balancing personal responsibility and social protection.

stimuli.text:
Retirement security is often discussed as a question of how much money individuals accumulate during their working lives. Yet the ability to enjoy financial independence in old age depends on more than savings alone. It is shaped by the stability of employment, the accessibility of financial institutions, the design of pension systems and the capacity of households to manage uncertainty over several decades.
Traditional pension arrangements were generally developed around the assumption that workers would enjoy relatively stable careers and predictable earnings. However, changing labour markets have weakened this assumption. A growing number of individuals experience irregular incomes, frequent changes in employment or prolonged periods outside the workforce. For such workers, maintaining consistent pension contributions can be difficult, even when they recognise the importance of retirement planning.
Financial inclusion is therefore not merely a matter of opening pension accounts. Participation must be sustained through affordable contributions, convenient payment mechanisms, transparent information and confidence in the institutions managing retirement savings. Excessive complexity may discourage participation, while poorly understood investment risks can undermine trust, particularly among individuals with limited financial knowledge.
Pension policy also involves difficult choices. Greater investment flexibility may improve opportunities for long-term wealth creation, but it can expose subscribers to market fluctuations. Guaranteed benefits may provide certainty, yet their financing must remain sustainable. Similarly, early access to accumulated savings may help households during emergencies but reduce the resources available after retirement.
These challenges affect different groups unequally. Women, informal workers and individuals with interrupted careers may accumulate smaller retirement balances despite spending many years engaged in economically valuable activities. A well-designed pension framework must recognise such differences without compromising financial sustainability or creating excessive administrative burdens.
Ultimately, the success of a pension system should not be judged solely by the number of accounts opened or the total assets accumulated. Its deeper purpose is to provide reliable income security in old age while balancing individual responsibility, social protection and long-term economic sustainability.

Illustrative title: Retirement Security in a Changing Economy
Model précis: Retirement security depends not simply on accumulated savings but also on stable earnings, accessible institutions and systems that manage uncertainty. Traditional pensions assumed predictable employment, whereas irregular incomes and interrupted careers now make regular contributions difficult. Genuine financial inclusion therefore requires affordable, convenient and transparent arrangements that build trust. Policymakers must balance investment flexibility against market risk, guarantees against financial sustainability, and emergency withdrawals against future adequacy. Women, informal workers and those with interrupted careers face particular disadvantages, calling for inclusive yet administratively sustainable designs. Pension systems should consequently be assessed not only by enrolment or assets, but by their ability to provide dependable old-age income while balancing personal responsibility and social protection.

B, 4.3% of GDP, is the FY 2026–27 Budget Estimate for fiscal deficit. C (4.4%) belongs to a different Budget-period comparison; A and D are not the specified BE figure. A ignores the write-down; B ignores selling expenses; D incorrectly adds expenses. The rule is lower of cost and NRV, not lower of cost and selling price.

B is controlling: measure actual performance, compare it with standards, identify deviations and take corrective action. Planning sets objectives (A), staffing secures people (C), and organising allocates roles/resources (D). Controlling is the feedback-and-correction function, not simply drawing up a plan. The question’s decisive clue is comparison of actual results with standards followed by corrective action.

D. For an existing fixed-coupon bond, higher market price means lower yield to maturity and vice versa, other inputs held constant. A reverses the relationship; B denies the price sensitivity of yield; C confuses the contractually fixed coupon rate with the changing market yield. B, 1,200 units. Contribution per unit = ₹500 selling price − ₹300 variable cost = ₹200. Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit = ₹2,40,000 / ₹200 = 1,200. A and B mistakenly impose exercise obligations on the buyer; C describes the buyer of a call option. The seller/writer, not the buyer, undertakes the corresponding obligation if valid exercise occurs. Put = right to sell; call = right to buy.

B. Activity-based costing first groups overhead by activity, then charges products using an activity cost driver such as number of set-ups. A uses a broad allocation base regardless of the actual driver; C marginal costing focuses on variable contribution and does not solve this overhead-driver allocation; D equivalent-unit process costing addresses homogeneous production. Allocate set-up cost by set-ups when set-ups cause that overhead.

C. Section 63 allows eligible free reserves, the securities premium account and the capital redemption reserve account to be capitalised for fully paid bonus shares, subject to conditions. It expressly excludes reserves created by asset revaluation. Hence A, B and D name eligible sources, while C is prohibited. Exam trap: an accounting reserve appearing in equity is not automatically distributable or eligible for bonus capitalisation.

B, 110. GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP × 100 = 2,200 / 2,000 × 100. A (90.9) inverts the ratio; C treats the figure as a percentage by an incorrect operation; D omits the base-100 scaling. A value of 110 indicates the current-price level of measured output is 10% above the base-year price level in this calculation.

B. APY offers specified Government-guaranteed minimum monthly pensions of ₹1,000, ₹2,000, ₹3,000, ₹4,000 or ₹5,000 after age 60, subject to enrolment and contribution conditions. A gives the wrong amount and age; C wrongly denies the defined guarantee; D wrongly presents a lump-sum at age 40. Do not confuse APY’s specified minimum benefit with ordinary market-linked NPS accumulation.

C. Excellent training accuracy with much weaker performance on independent representative data suggests overfitting or poor generalisation. A underfitting would usually show weak training performance too; B accuracy alone cannot guarantee data integrity; D successful cross-validation cannot be inferred from one reported test result. Look at the gap between in-sample and out-of-sample performance, not the training score alone.

B. Behavioural microtargeting creates privacy and profiling concerns, particularly when personal data and tailored messages can be used manipulatively. A spectrum licensing, C copyright ownership and D circulation audit may be genuine media-law subjects, but none responds as directly to individual behavioural profiling. The ethical issue is not personalisation as such; it is data use, consent, fairness and manipulation risk.

B, active listening and clarification. Paraphrasing another person’s concern and checking accuracy verifies shared understanding. A one-way persuasion seeks to influence rather than clarify; C avoids the feedback just used; D selectively withholds information. The question gives two clues: restating in one’s own words and seeking confirmation. Together they distinguish genuine listening from passive silence.

A. Under PFRDA Act Section 51, the Central Government may make rules; Section 52 empowers PFRDA to make regulations consistent with the Act and rules. B and C incorrectly give both law-making powers to one institution; D reverses their statutory roles. Rules and regulations are both subordinate instruments, but the maker and statutory delegation differ. Do not confuse a regulator’s circulars with its regulations.

D, 6.8–7.2%, is the Economic Survey 2025–26 projection for real GDP growth in FY 2026–27. A and B are below this stated projection, while C is above it. The Survey figure is a forward-looking range, not a realised FY27 growth rate. In dynamic-data questions, first identify whether the number is an estimate, projection or actual and then match the fiscal year.

C, 2.20:1. Initial current ratio = 480/240 = 2. After paying ₹40 lakh of current payables from cash, current assets become ₹440 lakh and current liabilities ₹200 lakh. New ratio = 440/200 = 2.2. B wrongly assumes the ratio is unchanged; A and D reflect incorrect adjustments. Paying liabilities from cash increases an initially above-one current ratio under the stated assumptions.

D. In Herzberg’s two-factor theory, pay and working conditions are hygiene factors: their inadequacy causes dissatisfaction, while their adequacy does not automatically produce intrinsic satisfaction. Achievement, responsibility and recognition are more typical motivators. A incorrectly calls salary necessarily intrinsic, B misclassifies recognition, and C claims an automatic long-term motivating effect from working conditions. Avoid equating the absence of dissatisfaction with positive motivation.

A, 12%. CAPM required return = risk-free rate + beta × (market return − risk-free rate) = 6% + 1.2 × (11% − 6%) = 12%. B ignores beta-adjusted premium; C typically results from multiplying by the wrong base; D incorrectly adds beta times the full market return. The market risk premium is 5 percentage points, not 11%.

B, flexible budgeting, adjusts variable and other activity-dependent budget amounts to the actual 12,000-unit output. A retains the original static activity assumption; C confuses zero-based justification of expenditures with activity-flexing; D addresses allocation among competing capital projects. A fixed budget is useful for initial planning, but comparing actual costs with an activity-adjusted flexible budget isolates efficiency from volume differences.

A. Section 123 permits the Board of Directors to declare an interim dividend, subject to statutory conditions. B refers to shareholder approval associated with final dividends, not the Board’s interim power. C can review financial information but does not itself declare the dividend; D, the auditor, expresses an audit opinion rather than taking the Board’s distribution decision. Separate authority to recommend, approve and declare dividends.

D, 5. In the simple closed-economy Keynesian model, government-expenditure multiplier = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/(1 − 0.8) = 5. A is the reciprocal of MPC; B and C do not follow the stated formula. The result relies on the question’s assumptions: leakage through taxes or imports, or other changes in behaviour, would reduce the multiplier.

C. A conventional life annuity transfers the contractual longevity/payment-duration risk to the insurer: payments continue according to the contract even if the annuitant lives longer than expected. A employment eligibility, B the retiree’s other equity portfolio risk and D tax-law changes are not the principal risk transferred. The annuity does not by itself eliminate inflation or insurer counterparty risk.

A. An agentic system can select and sequence actions, use tools, observe feedback and iterate toward a specified goal. B a longer one-off output and D ranking drafts can occur without multi-step agency; C is a training method, not a defining property of agentic operation. Agentic does not mean ungoverned or independently self-directed: constraints, permissions and human oversight still matter.

C. Section 14 expressly empowers PFRDA to register and regulate pension intermediaries. A wrongly treats PFRDA as the guarantor of all market-linked pension returns; B confuses regulation with selecting an individual subscriber’s investments under NPS Active Choice; D confuses the Authority with the Central Recordkeeping Agency, which maintains subscriber/PRAN records. Distinguish the regulator’s powers from functions of supervised intermediaries and decisions reserved to subscribers.

D. Effective capital expenditure in BE 2026–27 was ₹17.15 lakh crore: direct GoI capital spending ₹12.22 lakh crore plus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets ₹4.93 lakh crore. A and C leave out one of these components; B mistakes the direct capex subtotal for the effective total. A grant that creates a capital asset expands effective capex even though it is classified differently in Union accounts.

B, financing cash inflow. Issuing equity raises funds from owners and therefore changes financing, not operations or investment. A would involve the company’s main revenue-generating activity; C usually concerns buying/selling long-term assets or investments; D applies when no cash actually changes hands. Share issuance for cash is a financing receipt even if the proceeds are later spent on capital equipment.

C, a supporting/participating style, because employees are technically competent yet need consultation and encouragement. A directing provides too much task instruction; B coaching retains more task direction than needed; D delegating withdraws support despite the stated participation need. Situational leadership varies direction and support with competence and commitment; high skill does not always imply low need for relationship support.

B. A repo-rate cut can lower banks’ marginal funding cost and, with effective transmission, make borrowing and investment more attractive. A incorrectly assumes a mechanical one-for-one reduction in every lending rate; C reverses the expected monetary direction; D confuses repo policy with the independent CRR instrument. Actual credit growth depends on risk appetite, demand, liquidity and transmission, so the question correctly says potentially.

C, ₹6,000 adverse. Material price variance = (standard price − actual price) × actual quantity = (₹60 − ₹66) × 1,000 = −₹6,000. Under the stated sign convention a negative result is adverse because the firm paid ₹6/kg above standard. A reverses the favourable/adverse label; B uses the wrong magnitude; D is neither the difference nor the correct sign.

A. Section 143 gives the statutory auditor access to the company’s books and vouchers at all times for audit purposes. B declaring dividends and C appointing directors are governance decisions, not audit powers. D wrongly makes statutory inspection dependent on a fresh shareholder resolution. Auditors may seek information and explanations, but access and audit opinion do not make them the company’s management.

C. Ordinary personal remittances from non-residents to residents are recorded as secondary-income transfers in the current account. A foreign direct investment, B external commercial borrowing and D reserve-asset transactions fall in the financial account under BPM6, rather than being personal transfers. The capital account is a separate category mainly for capital transfers and non-produced non-financial assets; do not collapse capital and financial accounts.

B. Ordinary NPS is a defined-contribution, market-linked arrangement: benefits depend on contributions, accumulated investment returns and the applicable exit/annuitisation rules. A describes a final-salary defined-benefit formula; C invents a universal government guarantee across NPS assets; D wrongly gives everyone the same annuity regardless of corpus. Do not confuse NPS with APY’s guaranteed minimum options or separate government pension arrangements.

A. Section 149’s independent-director test uses detailed conditions involving promoter/management connections, pecuniary relationships and other eligibility criteria. B mere minority nomination, C non-executive status and D length of service do not by themselves establish statutory independence. Independence is substantive, not a title; relevant relationships and disqualifications must be checked against the law and applicable rules.

A, the secondary market. Investors trade securities already issued, transferring ownership without the issuer necessarily receiving fresh capital. B the primary market raises new funds by issuance; C IPO and D new subscription are specific primary-issue mechanisms. A securities exchange is commonly a secondary-market venue, whereas applying to a fresh public issue belongs to the primary market.

D, rights issue. Under Section 62, a company offering further shares for cash to existing equity shareholders in proportion to holdings is ordinarily making a rights offer. A bonus shares involve capitalising eligible reserves rather than fresh cash; B employee options target employees under an incentive plan; C IPO offers securities to the public as an initial listing. The decisive clues are existing shareholders and proportionate cash subscription.

B, 1.0 in absolute value. Quantity falls by 20/200 = 10%; price rises by 10/100 = 10%; PED = −10%/10% = −1, so absolute elasticity is 1. A, C and D use incorrect percentage bases or ratios. The question specifies original-value percentage changes; midpoint/arc elasticity would differ slightly, so do not silently change the convention.

C. A lifecycle fund normally tapers equity exposure as retirement approaches to reduce vulnerability to equity-market swings when time for recovery is shorter. A incorrectly increases risk with age as a supposed necessity; B mistakes risk reduction for a benefit guarantee; D confuses strategy design with a promise to replicate historical returns. Changing the allocation cannot eliminate all market, interest-rate or inflation risk.

D: both statements are correct. Section 173(1) generally requires at least four Board meetings a year and no more than 120 days between consecutive meetings, subject to statutory exemptions. Section 410 constitutes the NCLAT, while Section 421 provides for appeals against NCLT orders. A omits the true appellate statement; B omits the true meeting rule; C wrongly rejects both. Do not cite Section 410 alone for the right of appeal.

A, 61.5% of nominal GDP, is the Economic Survey 2025–26 figure for private final consumption expenditure in FY 2025–26 using first advance estimates. B, C and D are not that reported share. Note the precision of the label: the Survey also cites 61.4% for H1 FY26, which must not be confused with the full-year FAE 61.5%. Estimates can later be revised.
